They generally employ a key module known as the cost volume module, which creates an initial cost volume by comparing a current frame and a subsequent frame. However, this initial volume often lacks sufficient similarity due to significant positional disparities between the two frames, ultimately hindering the performance of subsequent CNN modules. To address this issue, we introduce a novel cost volume module that dynamically adjusts the cost volume based on estimated optical flow. deep learning models have gained popularity, allowing them to address a wide range of issues simultaneously. However, in reality, machines and humans often focus on the most pressing tasks at any given time. This concept is known as the "priority of tasks." Inspired by this idea, we introduce a novel training strategy for multi-task models, which prioritizes tasks dynamically based on their performance. Our approach, which adapts to the data distribution, enables efficient training of models for various priority settings. Through comprehensive testing, we demonstrate that this method yields better results on multiple benchmark datasets when tasks are prioritized effectively. Conversely, when tasks have equal importance, we observe performance comparable to standard training methods. Furthermore, we showcase the practical applications of task prioritization in real-world scenarios, such as image captioning and multi-language machine translation. Our findings are backed by experimental results, which highlight the potential benefits of this approach. The code is available on the GitHub repository https://github.com/zhengruihc/DynPrior. By combining data from Gaia EDR3 and clusters with comprehensive proper motion information, we identify the most distant stars that are likely to be members of each cluster. We then apply a two-step process to calculate sodium-abundance variations, first accounting for the distribution of non-member stars in the region and, if necessary, applying a correction based on the radial velocity distribution of member stars. Our results reveal significant sodium-abundance variations within several clusters, including NGC 3202, NGC 4590, NGC 5288, NGC 6106, and NGC 6266. These variations are particularly pronounced in the more metal-poor clusters NGC 4590 and NGC 6106, where the range of sodium-abundance variations exceeds the measurement uncertainty. We discuss the implications of these findings in the context of the early formation and chemical evolution of these clusters. Our method is expected to facilitate the identification of additional clusters exhibiting sodium-abundance variations, particularly those with fewer than ten stars with measured sodium-abundance variations. Furthermore, this method can be adapted to investigate other chemical abundance variations in stars within globular clusters. This paper investigates the existence of solutions to rate-independent systems that incorporate nonlinearity and a spatially-dependent limit case of damping. Our approach focuses on two distinct models: one describing a viscoelastic behavior and the other accounting for plasticity. By establishing well-posedness results in a Hilbert space, we demonstrate the existence of weak entropy solutions using a time-discretization method. Our analysis includes an in-depth convergence assessment of fully-discrete approximations to the exact solution. The method employed in this study can also be applied to solving systems with nonlinear dependence on the memory term. Furthermore, our work expands on existing results from \cite{Kliegl2021}, with the added benefit of allowing for a fully-discrete scheme that is independent of the time-step size. Lastly, our study provides a strong-convergence result for the approximated solutions, with the rate of convergence depending on the time-step size. The results obtained are verified through both theoretical analysis and numerical simulations. The latter, in particular, highlights the necessity of using a backward difference formula for the time discretization in order to ensure the satisfaction of the entropy inequality. Our numerical experiments demonstrate that using other time discretization methods, such as the Runge-Kutta method, results in the approximated solution failing to meet the required conditions. The results of this study are expected to contribute significantly to the development of efficient numerical methods for solving rate-independent systems with spatially-dependent structural damping. Our investigation focuses on the fundamental question of whether it is possible to train a hidden Markov model from a single student's data without access to broader population statistics.  We examine this issue within the context of a simplified, single-variable Markov state transition model, where each student's knowledge progression is represented by a hidden sequence of skill states and actual exam results serve as observable data.  Our study reveals that the hidden Markov model can indeed be trained from individual student data, but this training is contingent upon the existence of a sufficient number of errors in recorded exam results.
